subject: maths
title: Speed, distance and time

slides.heading: Speed, distance and time — the most used rate of change
slides.body: Speed measures how quickly distance is covered — it is distance divided by time. All three quantities are linked: know any two and you can find the third. The units must be consistent: if speed is in km/h, distance must be in km and time must be in hours — convert minutes to hours before substituting. Average speed over a whole journey is always total distance ÷ total time, not the average of the individual speeds.
slides.note: Maximum 3 sentences. Plain English. No AQA references. What is this and why does it matter.

slides.heading: The speed–distance–time triangle
slides.formula: Distance = Speed × Time | Speed = Distance ÷ Time | Time = Distance ÷ Speed
slides.formulaExplained: Distance = Speed × Time. Cover the one you want to find to see the formula: cover D to get S × T; cover S to get D ÷ T; cover T to get D ÷ S. Time must be in the same unit throughout — convert minutes to hours by dividing by 60 (e.g. 45 min = 0.75 h, not 0.45 h). For a journey in two parts, average speed = total distance ÷ total time — calculate each journey time separately, then add.
slides.whenToUse: Any question involving speed, distance and time — finding one given the other two, converting between units of time, or calculating average speed over a multi-stage journey.
slides.note: Show formula in standard notation. Explain each variable. State when this formula applies.

slides.heading: Let's work through one
slides.question: A bus travels 126 km in 1 hour 30 minutes. Calculate the average speed in km/h.

steps.instruction: Convert the time to hours. 1 hour 30 minutes = 1 + 30/60 hours.

slides.note: Numbers must differ from any question in the question bank for this subtopic.

slides.heading: Watch out for this

mistakes.mistake: Converting minutes to hours incorrectly — e.g. treating 1 hour 20 minutes as 1.2 hours instead of 1.333... hours (1 + 20/60).
mistakes.correction: Divide minutes by 60 to convert to hours: 20 min = 20/60 = 1/3 h ≈ 0.333 h. Never just place the minutes after a decimal point — that only works for exact half-hours.

mistakes.mistake: Calculating average speed as the mean of two speeds — e.g. for a journey of 40 km at 20 km/h then 60 km at 30 km/h, writing (20 + 30) ÷ 2 = 25 km/h.
mistakes.correction: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. Find each leg's time separately (t₁ = 40/20 = 2 h, t₂ = 60/30 = 2 h), then: 100 ÷ 4 = 25 km/h. The shortcut of averaging speeds only gives the right answer by coincidence in specific cases.

mistakes.mistake: Inverting the formula — calculating time ÷ distance instead of distance ÷ time for speed, giving an answer in hours/km instead of km/h.
mistakes.correction: Use the triangle: cover Speed, and what remains is D on top and T on the bottom — S = D ÷ T. Check the units: speed should be in km/h or m/s, not h/km.

slides.note: Minimum 2, maximum 3 mistakes. Specific not generic.

keyFacts.fact: Distance = Speed × Time. Cover the quantity you want: D = S × T, S = D ÷ T, T = D ÷ S.
keyFacts.examTip: Write the triangle at the top of your working for every question. It takes 2 seconds and prevents formula errors.

keyFacts.fact: Always convert time to hours before substituting. Minutes ÷ 60 = hours. 45 min = 0.75 h. 1h 20min = 1.333... h.
keyFacts.examTip: Never write 1h 20min as 1.20 h — that treats 20 minutes as 20 hundredths of an hour, which is wrong.

keyFacts.fact: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. Calculate each part's time separately, then add all times and all distances.
keyFacts.examTip: The average of two speeds is not the average speed. Always use total distance ÷ total time.

note: keyFacts: 2-4 entries. Exam-precise language. These are what Mabel writes into her notes.
